_meta: A deep stack of residual blocks and the initial gain of each block's residual branch, used to show why zero-initializing the last layer of each residual branch -- so the branch outputs zero at initialization and the block computes x + 0 = x, the identity -- keeps the signal magnitude constant through depth, whereas a standard nonzero-initialized branch perturbs the signal at every block and the perturbations compound exponentially with depth. A residual block computes x + f(x): the input flows through unchanged on the skip connection, plus whatever the residual branch f adds. At the very start of training f's weights are random, so f(x) is some nonzero perturbation of x, and stacking N blocks multiplies the signal by (1 + branch_gain) N times -- the same exponential-in-depth compounding that makes initialization scale matter, now riding on top of the residual path. If instead the final layer of each residual branch is initialized to zero, f(x) is exactly zero at init, every block is x + 0 = x, and the entire network is the identity function at step zero, no matter how deep. That is the ideal starting point for a residual network: the signal passes through untouched, gradients are well-behaved, and training begins by gently moving the branches away from zero rather than fighting a signal that has already exploded or drifted through dozens of layers. x0 is the input signal magnitude; branch_gain is the residual branch's effective multiplier under standard init; depth is the number of stacked blocks (a second, deeper depth is also examined). These are the fixture; the output magnitude under standard init vs zero-init, at the given depth and a deeper one, are computed.
